metadata.title: Examining the context of better science literacy outcomes among U.S. schools using visual analytics: A machine learning approach
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 school-level aggregates derived from student, teacher, and principal questionnaires, focusing on 238 U.S. schools. The manuscript describes aggregation to the school level, standardization of continuous variables, and outlier checking, but it does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the analysis. Because the analysis is based on multidimensional scaling (MDS) preference analysis and subsequent ANOVA on school-level quadrant groupings, the paper does not specify any complex-survey variance estimation or weight variable usage. As a result, readers should treat the reported variance explained and significance tests as descriptive/analytic results rather than fully design-based population estimates unless weights are confirmed in the original PISA technical documentation or the authors’ analysis code.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a school-level science literacy outcome constructed by aggregating student science test scores to the school level, but the paper does not describe whether these scores are PV-based (and if so, how PVs were combined) or whether any PV handling was performed. Additionally, the manuscript does not report any missing-data strategy for questionnaire-derived scales or for the aggregated science literacy outcome. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically include missing questionnaire responses and require an explicit approach (e.g., complete-case exclusion or imputation) to ensure reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 data with a school-level analytic unit: 238 U.S. schools. The study aggregated student and teacher questionnaire variables to the school level (because teacher and student data are nested within schools) and constructed 49 school-context variables from principal, teacher, and student questionnaires. Continuous variables were standardized (mean 0, SD 1), and outliers were checked with no outliers found. The paper does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., missing questionnaire handling, minimum response thresholds, or whether schools with missing components were excluded), so the exact analytic subsample construction beyond the 238 schools is not fully documented.

main_findings.performance_metrics: MDS preference analysis (visual quadrant classification) + ANOVA: quadrant grouping explained 46% of variance in school science literacy outcomes; ANOVA F(4233)=50.24, p<.001; Quadrant 4 differed from other quadrants (ps<0.001), especially Quadrant 1; Quadrant 3 variables showed no vector length (poor model fit).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science data aggregated to the school level for 238 U.S. schools, the study leveraged individualized instruction, student science self-efficacy, achievement motivation, enjoyment of science, and creative extra-curricular activities to characterize school positions in an MDS preference plot and to classify schools into quadrants, finding that schools in Quadrant 4 (reflecting these positive characteristics) had substantially higher science literacy outcomes than schools in other quadrants, with quadrant grouping accounting for 46% of variance (ANOVA F(4233)=50.24, p<.001). This indicates that strengthening individualized science instruction and students’ motivational/affective engagement may be a practical pathway for improving schoolwide science literacy, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study used PISA 2015 science data aggregated to the school level for 238 U.S. schools, constructing 49 school-context variables from principal, teacher, and student questionnaires. It applied MDS preference analysis (a visual analytics approach) to map schools and variables into a two-dimensional space, then divided the plot into four quadrants and tested quadrant differences using one-way ANOVA. Schools in Quadrant 4—characterized by higher individualized teaching, student science self-efficacy, achievement motivation, enjoyment of science, creative extra-curricular activities, and a more qualified science teaching force—showed much higher science literacy outcomes than schools in other quadrants. Quadrant grouping explained 46% of the variance in school science literacy outcomes (F(4233)=50.24, p<.001), with Quadrant 4 differing from other quadrants (ps<0.001). Limitations include the absence of reported PV-handling and missing-data strategy, and the fact that the approach is primarily descriptive/visual rather than a validated predictive ML model.
